content.intro: Learn connection management and pooling through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Connection Management and Pooling matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Professional work with connection management and pooling means that another person can review, repeat, and safely operate the query. Keep formatting consistent, test meaningful edge cases, use versioned migrations, and document engine/version assumptions.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Connection lifecycle, Connection pools, Pool sizing concepts, Connection timeouts. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Connection lifecycle
items.text: Connection lifecycle is part of a repeatable development workflow. Use a dedicated local lab, check the connection target before running changes, save scripts in version control, and keep credentials out of source files.

items.title: Pool sizing concepts
items.text: Pool sizing concepts helps you build professional workflows for SQL style, static analysis, tests, migrations, application integration, connection pooling, and pagination. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Connection timeouts
items.text: Connection timeouts needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Transactions and pooled connections
items.text: Transactions and pooled connections is about keeping multi-step work correct when errors or other sessions intervene. Keep transactions short, define what must succeed together, handle conflicts explicitly, and test using separate sessions in a disposable database.

items.title: Preventing connection leaks
items.text: Preventing connection leaks is part of a repeatable development workflow. Use a dedicated local lab, check the connection target before running changes, save scripts in version control, and keep credentials out of source files.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic connection lifecycle and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
